parts.title: The oldest tree in the village
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
In the middle of our village stands a huge oak tree. Nobody knows exactly how old it is, but people say that it is more than six hundred years old. Its trunk is so wide that five children can stand round it with their arms stretched out.

When I was small, the oak was the centre of everything. We played hide-and-seek among its roots, and in summer the whole village had picnics in its shade. My grandfather told me that, long ago, farmers held meetings under its branches.

Two years ago, a terrible storm broke one of the biggest branches. The villagers were very upset. Some people thought that the tree was dying and wanted to cut it down for safety. But an expert came from the city and examined it. He said that the oak was strong and healthy and would live for many more years.

Since then, we have taken better care of it. We built a low fence round the roots, to protect them from visitors' feet, and every spring, children come to measure it. Last year, I measured it with my own daughter, and she asked me, "Will it still be here when I am as old as you?" I hope so.

questions.explanation: People say it is more than six hundred years old.

parts.title: Why forests matter
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Forests cover almost one third of the land on Earth. [1] They are home to more than half of all the animals and plants that live on land.

Trees also help us breathe. [2] During the day, their leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air and give back oxygen, which people and animals need.

Forests protect the soil too. [3] Without roots to hold the earth together, heavy rain can wash it away and cause floods.

Sadly, every year, millions of hectares of forest disappear. [4] Farmers, builders and companies cut them down to make space or to sell the wood.

However, there is some good news. [5] In many countries, people are planting new trees and creating protected areas where nothing may be cut down.
sentences: Roots keep it firmly in place.
Large areas are lost for ever.
The air in a forest is very clean.
Nature is slowly beginning to recover in some places.
They are found on every continent except Antarctica.
The smaller trees grow faster than the large ones.

gaps.explanation: Forests are found on every continent; the next sentence goes on with "They are home to" more than half of all animals and plants.
The air in a forest is clean; the next sentence says trees give back oxygen.
Roots keep the soil in place; the next sentence says without roots rain washes it away.
Large areas are lost for ever; the next sentence says farmers and builders cut them down.
Nature is recovering in some places; the next sentence says people are planting trees.

parts.title: A message from the woods
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Nim, I am writing this from a camp in the middle of a forest. We arrived [1] Friday evening, and we put up our tents before dark. The air smells wonderful, [2] it is colder than I expected. Last night, we sat round a fire and [3] stories until midnight. This morning, I heard a strange noise. It was a deer, [4] was eating leaves near my tent! I wish you [5] here with us. We are staying until Sunday, so there is still time for you to [6] us. Auden

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: We use on with days of the week.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: But shows contrast: the air is lovely but cold.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: We tell stories, so the verb is told.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: Which is used for an animal in a relative clause.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: I wish you were here is the pattern for an unreal wish.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: Join us means to come and be with us.

parts.title: Planting a tree
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Planting a tree is a simple way to help the planet. First, choose a tree that suits your garden. Some trees grow very tall, [1] others stay small, so it is important to read the label. Dig a hole that is twice as wide as the roots. Put the tree in the hole and fill it [2] earth, pressing it down gently. Water it well, and keep watering it every week for the first year. Many people forget this, [3] their young trees die. It is also a good idea to put a stick next to the tree [4] hold it up in strong winds. In a few years, you will see birds visiting your tree, and one day, it may be [5] large that it gives shade in summer. Planting a tree is something [6] will be good for people for a hundred years.

gaps.explanation: While shows contrast between tall trees and small trees.
We fill a hole with earth.
So shows the result: people forget, so trees die.
A stick to hold it up gives the purpose.
So large that it gives shade.
That refers to something and begins the relative clause.

parts.title: A radio message about a forest festival
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: presenter
turns.text: Welcome back to the afternoon show. This weekend, the town is holding its annual Forest Festival in Green Park. It begins on Saturday at ten in the morning and finishes on Sunday evening. There will be music from local bands, and the famous storyteller Mrs Dale will read tales about woodland animals. Children can paint their faces and make nests out of leaves. There will also be a competition for the best wooden sculpture, and the winner will receive a hundred pounds. Entry is free, but visitors are asked to bring a bag for their rubbish. Parking is limited, so please come by bus. The number six bus stops right outside the park. If it rains, the festival moves to the sports hall. I hope to see you all there!

parts.title: An interview with a forest ranger
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Tove, you work as a forest ranger. What is a normal day like?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: There is no normal day. Every day is different. I might repair a path in the morning, rescue a lost walker at lunchtime and count owls at night.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the best part of the job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The silence. In a big forest, early in the morning, you hear only birds and the wind. It is like a church.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the worst part?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Litter. People leave bottles, bags and even mattresses. Last month, I found a washing machine.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Have you ever been scared?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Once, in winter, I got caught in a snowstorm. I built a shelter from branches and waited until morning.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is your advice for people who visit forests?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Tell someone where you are going, take water and a charged phone, and never walk alone after dark.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you have a favourite tree?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: A huge old beech near the north gate. I say hello to it every day. My colleagues think I am mad.

questions.prompt: What does Tove say about her days?
questions.explanation: She says there is no normal day.

questions.prompt: What does she like best?
options: The silence early in the morning
questions.explanation: She loves the silence in the early morning.

questions.prompt: What annoys her most?
questions.explanation: She says the worst part is litter.

questions.prompt: What did she do in the snowstorm?
questions.explanation: She built a shelter from branches.

questions.prompt: What is her advice about phones?
questions.explanation: She says to take water and a charged phone.

questions.prompt: What does she do every day?
questions.explanation: She says hello to her favourite beech tree every day.
